Given an array of n integers (n up to 200000, values fitting in int64), answer q queries of the form (l, r, k): among the elements at positions l..r inclusive, return the k-th smallest DISTINCT value, or -1 if fewer than k distinct values exist. q is up to 200000. Both l..r and k vary per query, and the array is static.

Derive an algorithm that answers all queries within a 2-second budget. State the complexity, prove the bound, describe the data structure precisely enough to implement it, and then work through the concrete case n=8, a=[3,1,3,4,1,5,9,2], with the three queries (1,5,2), (2,7,3) and (4,4,2), showing the intermediate state at each step. Finally name the two inputs most likely to break a naive implementation and say why.

Write a single self-contained C++17 header that implements a fixed-capacity LRU cache with the following contract:
  - template<class K, class V>, no dependencies outside <unordered_map>, <list>, <optional>, <cstddef>
  - explicit capacity in the constructor, throws std::invalid_argument on 0
  - get(key) -> std::optional<V>, marks the entry most-recently-used
  - put(key, value) inserts or updates, evicts the least-recently-used entry when full
  - erase(key) -> bool, size(), capacity(), clear()
  - O(1) amortised for get, put and erase; no iterator invalidation for untouched entries
  - a peek(key) that does NOT change recency, for tests
Then write a set of unit tests as plain assert() calls in a main(), covering eviction order, update-does-not-grow, erase of the LRU head and tail, and the capacity-1 edge case. Explain each design decision in a short comment where it is not obvious.
